title: I like it — sentences that flip the subject
goal: Say what you like, need and feel — and learn the dative, the case of the receiver, plus one sentence pattern that makes the thing the subject and you the target.
bekal: using *sviđa mi se* and *sviđaju mi se* with the right verb form
using the dative pronouns *mi, ti, mu, joj, nam, vam, im* and their long forms

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kako ti se sviđa Sarajevo?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon on the office terrace; the city is starting to light up in the valley. Amina asks in the tone of someone who already knows the answer.

notes: ***Sviđa mi se Sarajevo* — the subject is Sarajevo, not me.** Literally "Sarajevo pleases me". So when the thing liked is plural, the verb goes plural too: *sviđaju mi se filmovi*. This is learners' most common mistake — *sviđa mi se filmovi* sounds as wrong to a native ear as "the films pleases me" does in English.

***Volim* vs *sviđa mi se*.** *Volim* takes a normal accusative and means a steady, strong liking: *Volim kafu* (I love coffee, always). *Sviđa mi se* is an impression — something appeals to you: *Sviđa mi se ova kafa* (this coffee is good). With people the difference is big and important: *Volim te* means **I love you**; *Sviđaš mi se* means **I like you, I'm attracted to you**. Don't mix them up.

***Meni* and *tebi* are long forms used for emphasis.** *Meni se sviđa kafa* = "as for me, it's the coffee I like" — there's an implied comparison. In ordinary conversation the short forms (*mi, ti*) are used, and they sit in second place like all the other little words.

***Poslat ću ti ga* — three little words neatly in a row.** *ću* (helping verb), *ti* (dative), *ga* (accusative) — exactly the order of the table in Unit 12. A sentence like this will feel impossible now and natural in two months; what matters is that you can read it.

**Ajvar.** A relish of roasted red peppers and eggplant, cooked for hours and bottled every autumn. Every Bosnian family has its own recipe, and asking someone for their ajvar recipe is a serious compliment. The hot version is called *ljuti ajvar* — the closest thing to a chili sauce you'll find on a Bosnian table.

grammars.title: The dative — the receiver form
body: The fourth case, and the cheapest of all: **its form is exactly the same as the locative** you learned in Unit 9. So what you learn here isn't a new form but a new job.
after: **The difference between dative and locative is not the form but the job.** The locative **always** has a preposition in front (*u gradu, na poslu, o Bosni*). The dative usually has **no** preposition at all — it marks the receiver: *Dajem bratu*, *Pišem sestri*, *Hvala vam*. Two prepositions take the dative: *prema* (toward, regarding) and *ka / k* (to — rare in conversation).

**The same sound changes as in the locative:** *majka → majci*, *knjiga → knjizi*, *Amerika → Americi*. **k → c, g → z, h → s** before the ending *-i*. You saw this pattern in Unit 9; here it comes back exactly the same.
**Dative pronouns have two sets, just like accusative pronouns:**

**short** — *mi, ti, mu, joj, nam, vam, im* — used every day, sitting in second place: *Daj mi. Reci mu. Hvala vam.* **long** — *meni, tebi, njemu, njoj, nama, vama, njima* — used for emphasis and after prepositions: *Meni se sviđa. Dođi k meni.*

**Verbs that most often pair with the dative:** *dati* (give), *reći* (say, tell), *pisati* (write to), *pomoći* (help — yes, in Bosnian you help **to** someone), *javiti se* (get in touch), *vjerovati* (believe, trust), *nedostajati* (be missing → be missed). Note *pomoći mu*, not *pomoći ga* — one of the few places that isn't what you'd expect.

grammars.title: Sentences that flip the subject
body: A group of Bosnian sentences makes **the person the receiver** and **the thing felt the subject**. Once you see the pattern, a dozen everyday expressions open up at once.
after: **The verb agrees with the thing felt, not the person.** *Sviđa mi se **kafa*** (singular) but *Sviđaju mi se **filmovi*** (plural). *Treba mi **odmor*** but *Trebaju mi **papiri***. If you remember one thing from this unit, make it this — it's the only part that really goes wrong often.

**Almost all bodily feelings and moods use this pattern:** *toplo mi je* (I'm hot), *muka mi je* (I feel sick), *strah me je* (I'm scared — this one takes the accusative), *lakše mi je* (I feel relieved), *svejedno mi je* (it's all the same to me).

**Saying you don't like something:** add *ne* as usual — *Ne sviđa mi se.* Or use a stronger word: *Mrzim…* (I hate), which Bosnians use much more lightly than English speakers use "hate" — *mrzim ponedjeljak* will shock no one.
**A useful scale:** *obožavam* (I adore) > *volim* (I love, I like) > *sviđa mi se* (I like it) > *može* (it'll do) > *ne sviđa mi se* (I don't like it) > *mrzim* (I hate).

blocks.text: Two patterns cover almost every conversation about hobbies: *Volim* + accusative, and *Volim* + dictionary form. *Volim muziku* (I love music), *Volim slušati muziku* (I love listening to music).

head: Sentence
English
rows: What do you like doing in your free time?
I like reading and listening to music.
I play soccer once a week.
It's all the same to me.
I don't have a hobby, I work too much.

blocks.title: Ćejf — a word that can't be translated
items: *Ćejf* (from Turkish *keyif*, related to Arabic *kayf*) means a slow pleasure you indulge in simply because you enjoy it — a cup of coffee sipped for half an hour, sitting by the river with no purpose, the first cigarette of the morning. The sentence: *To mi je ćejf.*

This word explains a lot about the Bosnian way of life, including why nobody rushes to finish their coffee. Use it correctly just once and people will turn their heads — hardly any foreigner knows it.
